chunks: What to monitor for battery safety. The question: What do you have to monitor in a battery to ensure it's operating safely?
To keep a battery safe, you monitor its voltage, current, and temperature all the time. For a lithium-ion cell, that means stopping the charge at about 4.
2 volts, stopping the discharge at about 3 volts, tripping fast on a short circuit, and avoiding charging when too cold or running when too hot.
You also watch slower things such as imbalance between cells. When a limit is hit, the protection opens a switch.
Think of a car dashboard and its safety systems. The gauges show speed, fuel, and engine temperature, and a warning light appears when something goes out of range.
A fuse protects the wiring if everything else fails.
A battery's protection circuit does the same: it watches the gauges, acts at the limits, and has a fuse or a PTC (a part that heats up and chokes off the current) as the last line.
The car picture lacks the speed: a short circuit needs a trip in microseconds.
A representative temperature-derating profile for charging.
No charge below the cold cutoff (lithium plating), reduced current in the cool band, full rate in the middle, reduced current when warm, and stop when hot.
Real numbers come from the cell datasheet and the charger IC's configuration; this shows the shape.
Overvoltage / undervoltage: a cell voltage too high (during charge) or too low (during discharge). Short-circuit protection: a fast trip when the current becomes dangerously high.
NTC thermistor: a sensor whose resistance falls as temperature rises.
Cell balancing: keeping the cells in a series pack at the same voltage ("Cell balancing: why, when, what if missing").
Protection circuit: the electronics that opens a switch when a limit is crossed.
A single lithium-ion cell is being charged. The monitor reads 4. 25 volts, above the 4. 2 volts target. It opens the series switch and the charge stops.
Another case: a short with 20 milliohms in the path from a 4 volts cell would try to push about 4 over 0. 02 equals 200 amps.
Only a hardware trip in microseconds to milliseconds can stop that in time. That is the whole idea.
"Voltage, current and temperature, continuously, per cell. Overvoltage around 4. 2 volts a cell and undervoltage around 3 volts. Overcurrent with a fast short-circuit trip.
Temperature with an NTC: no charging when it's near freezing, and cut off when it's hot. On top of that, cell imbalance, resistance growth and swelling.
If a limit is hit, open a MOSFET or contactor and stop the charger, and have a fuse as the backup."
